sections.title: Introduction
rules: In reinforcement learning, an autonomous agent learns by interacting with an environment.
The agent takes actions and receives feedback through scalar rewards or penalties.
There is no supervisor providing correct input-output target pairs.
Actions have long-term consequences that affect future states and delayed rewards.
The credit assignment problem involves identifying which past action produced a delayed reward.

sections.title: Single State Case: K-Armed Bandit
rules: The K-armed bandit is a non-associative reinforcement learning problem with a single state.
The agent chooses between K discrete actions, similar to slot machine levers.
Each action provides an uncertain reward from an unknown probability distribution.
The agent faces the exploration versus exploitation dilemma.
Exploitation selects the action with the highest estimated reward to maximize payoff.
Exploration selects alternate actions to discover more information about their true values.
The epsilon-greedy strategy exploits with high probability and explores randomly with probability epsilon.
Softmax exploration selects actions probabilistically using a Boltzmann distribution controlled by temperature.
Upper Confidence Bound algorithms add an exploration bonus based on parameter uncertainty.

sections.title: Elements of Reinforcement Learning
rules: We formulate the environment as a Markov Decision Process (MDP).
An MDP consists of states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor.
The Markov property assumes the next state depends only on the current state and action.
The discount factor balances immediate rewards against future rewards.
A policy maps each environmental state to an action.
The state-value function V(s) estimates expected cumulative return starting from state s.
The action-value function Q(s, a) estimates expected cumulative return taking action a in state s.
Bellman equations define recursive relationships between current values and expected future values.
The Bellman optimality equation characterizes the optimal value function and optimal policy.

sections.title: Model-Based Learning
rules: Model-based methods assume the agent knows or learns transition probabilities and reward distributions.
When model dynamics are known, dynamic programming algorithms compute the optimal policy.
Value iteration updates state values iteratively using the Bellman optimality operator.
Value iteration converges to optimal values because the Bellman operator is a contraction mapping.
Policy iteration alternates between two steps: policy evaluation and policy improvement.
Policy evaluation calculates state values for the current policy until convergence.
Policy improvement updates the policy greedily with respect to the evaluated values.
Policy iteration converges to the optimal policy in a finite number of iterations.

sections.title: Temporal Difference Learning
rules: Temporal difference (TD) methods learn directly from raw experience without an environment model.
TD learning bootstraps updates using current estimates without waiting for an episode to end.
The TD error is the difference between predicted value and updated estimate.
SARSA is an on-policy temporal difference control algorithm.
SARSA updates Q values using the action actually selected by the current behavioral policy.
Q-learning is an off-policy temporal difference control algorithm developed by Watkins.
Q-learning updates Q values using the maximum estimated reward of the next state.
Q-learning converges to the optimal action-value function independent of the exploration policy.
Eligibility traces bridge temporal difference learning and Monte Carlo methods.

sections.title: Generalization
rules: Tabular representations require storing a distinct value for every state-action pair.
Large or continuous state spaces make tabular storage infeasible.
Function approximation replaces lookup tables with parameterized models.
Linear function approximation computes values as a weighted combination of state feature vectors.
Neural networks and deep architectures serve as powerful nonlinear function approximators.
Deep Q-Networks (DQN) use convolutional networks to learn policies directly from raw sensory inputs.
Experience replay and target networks stabilize deep reinforcement learning updates.

sections.title: Partially Observable States
rules: In a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), the agent cannot directly view the state.
The agent receives noisy observations generated stochastically by the underlying state.
The agent maintains a belief state, which is a probability distribution over possible states.
The agent updates its belief state using Bayes' rule after each action and observation.
The Tiger problem illustrates POMDP decision making with listening actions and opening doors.
Solving POMDPs exactly is computationally intractable, requiring approximate heuristic algorithms.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Reinforcement learning combines concepts from animal psychology, optimal control, and dynamic programming.
Notable achievements include TD-Gammon for backgammon and AlphaGo for Go.
Policy gradient methods optimize policy parameters directly using gradient ascent on expected return.
